newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin restructures Russian cabinet, courts media.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin restructures Russian cabinet, courts media.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin promised on Friday to unveil the structure of Russia's new government and turned to the powerful media for support as he prepares for a painful leap forward in economic reform.

A major political rival, charismatic General Alexander Lebed, said social tension was now so high that violence could erupt anytime and the catalyst could be nationwide protests by trade unions on March 27.

Yeltsin has started a cabinet reshuffle to take account of public discontent and said he would issue a decree later on Friday restructuring the government, if not yet naming the new line-up. He will need all the help he can get from the media to ease tensions over the tough reforms he plans.
"Today your word may turn out to be extremely important, if not decisive," Yeltsin said in an appeal to journalists during a radio address.
The 66-year-old Kremlin leader, back in the Kremlin after months of illness, has said Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's old cabinet was unable to tackle the social and economic crisis.
He has also acknowledged that more then half of all Russians are unhappy with the state of affairs, but said improvements can be made only by completing stalled reforms.

Yeltsin has ordered Chernomyrdin to reshape the cabinet and sent his loyal lieutenant, Anatoly Chubais, to help the premier as his number two. On Friday he told media chiefs the new government would be smaller but more effective.
Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin as saying the new cabinet will have seven deputy prime ministers instead of the previous nine, and one first deputy premier instead of three.
"The most important thing is that the people who will come will have new, fresh ideas and thoughts," he said.
Yeltsin's decision to reshuffle the cabinet and speed up reforms has prompted an angry reaction in the communist-led State Duma lower house of parliament.

In a clear attack on Yeltsin, it passed at the first reading a resolution proclaiming October 4 -- the day on which in 1993 the president crushed hardline resistance by the Soviet-era parliament -- the "Day of the Defenders of the Constitution".
The new cabinet will face public discontent over long delays in wage and pension payments and the expected closure of many enterprises paralysed by non-payments.
Government handouts for education, health care, housing and municipal services may have to be cut.

Yeltsin's liberal aides acknowledge that such objectives cannot be attained in an impoverished country without serious social strains. The support of the media, which helped Yeltsin to re-election last year, could be vital.
The liberals who spearheaded the first phase of reforms five years ago became widely unpopular, partly because they failed to explain clearly to people why the changes were needed.
Lebed, a potentially strong presidential candidate, said the planned one-day nationwide protest action on March 27 could easily lead to anarchy.

"Little is needed for a few provocateurs to be introduced into any crowd during peaceful protest actions on March 27 -- broken shop windows, arson attacks, looted kiosks," said Lebed inaugurating his own Popular Republican Party.
"One victim and that's it," he added.

Yeltsin also used the meeting with the media chiefs to send a strong signal to the West -- and to a domestic audience -- that Russia wanted NATO to abandon any idea of integrating former Soviet republics into the Western defence alliance.

He said Russia would not make any concessions at a summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton in Helsinki next week that would threaten its defence capability. But he made clear Moscow was ready for a reasonable compromise.
